item.title: Why Won't the Tantrums Stop?
item.description:
Parenting

Why Won't the Tantrums Stop?

The science of co-regulation, what helps and when to ask for more help

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Tantrums fade as children build emotion regulation skills, which develop gradually over years.
  • Young children borrow a caregiver’s calm; repeated co-regulation helps them build their own self-regulation.
  • Staying steady is hard: empathy, your own upbringing, and parental stress all make calm harder to sustain.
  • If tantrums are frequent, prolonged, or unsafe, a pediatrician can direct further inquiry.

Tantrums, outbursts, meltdowns. These universal expressions of a young child's distress and overwhelm are uncomfortable for nearly all parents. They can come layered with embarrassment (especially in public), feelings of inadequacy and, in equal measure, frustration and exhaustion. Many parents turn to books, social media, friends, and doctors for an answer to the question often tinged with desperation: "How can I make this behavior stop?"

The general guidance is to keep a calm, grounded presence; to pair a warm tone with firm limits; and to look for underlying triggers such as hunger, fatigue, or a perceived injustice. It’s easier said than done, but for some families, getting these pieces right works wonders.

For others, it does not. A challenging emotional or behavioral cycle that repeats day after day can wear down even the most attuned and patient caregiver. Over time, the seeds of parental doubt, inadequacy, and disconnection can take root.

Here is the honest answer to the question in the title: tantrums are unlikely to disappear until a child develops the skills to regulate their emotions.

So the more useful questions are these:

  1. How can parents support and strengthen their child's self-regulation skills?
  2. When does a frequent or prolonged pattern of tantrums signal something more?
Source: Alizy Xiao/Unsplash

Emotion regulation is a skill that develops over years

Psychologist James Gross defined emotion regulation as “the processes by which individuals influence which emotions they have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions.” Children aren’t born with these skills, only the potential for them. They build gradually, through thousands of everyday exchanges with caregivers, as the brain matures. Emotion regulation is closely tied to executive function, the family of mental skills that lets us direct our thinking, attention, and behavior. It also depends on a growing ability to tolerate discomfort. Across infancy and toddlerhood, regulation is first supported by caregivers and only later managed by the child.

That makes caregivers central to the process. Early in life, while the brain’s regulatory systems are still developing, caregivers act as the child's external regulator. Predictable, safe care in the early years appears to shape the connections between the brain’s emotional centers and the prefrontal cortex, the wiring a child will later rely on to manage strong feelings.

In other words, the child "borrows" the caregiver's calm. Through repetition, those borrowed moments of soothing help build the child’s own capacity to settle. This back-and-forth is called co-regulation, and it gradually gives way to self-regulation as the child matures.

Your calm presence is a buffer

A parent's presence changes how a child's brain handles distress. In one small study, newborns held skin-to-skin by their mothers showed dampened pain-related brain activity in response to a heel prick, compared with newborns held while clothed.

The effect extends beyond infancy. In a brain-imaging study, simply seeing a photo of their mother, rather than a stranger, quieted children's amygdala reactivity. It also made their amygdala–prefrontal connections look more mature, and their behavioral regulation improved. The effect appeared in children but not in adolescents.

A parent's steady presence supports a child in distress, lending them regulatory capacity their own brain cannot yet supply.

What lending your calm looks like

In the moment:

  • Settle yourself first. A slow exhale, a lower voice, and getting down to your child's eye level signal safety before any words do.
  • Use fewer words. A brain in the middle of a meltdown can't process reasoning. Name the feeling briefly ("You're so mad the tower fell") and stop talking. Some children escalate when you name their feelings mid-storm; if yours does, save it for later and focus on your own composure.
  • Hold the line and keep everyone safe. Staying steady isn't the same as giving in. You can be warm while the answer remains no.
  • Wait it out nearby. Your presence is the intervention. Many children need you close but not touching until the peak has passed.
  • Reconnect afterward. A hug, a snack, a “that was a tough one.” Small moments of repair after a tantrum remind both of you that big feelings don’t break what you have.

In settled moments, where most of the learning happens:

  • Practice when everyone is at ease. Name feelings in books and play, rehearse a calm-down routine, try slow "blow out the candle" breathing together. Games like Red Light, Green Light, Simon Says, or freeze dance build inhibitory control, the ability to stop and wait, in a low-stakes way.
  • Reduce predictable triggers. Protect sleep and meals, give warnings before transitions, and keep daily routines consistent.
  • Notice the progress. Point out when your child waits, recovers faster, or uses words instead of hitting. Notice your own growing ability to stay steady in hard moments.

Why staying calm is so hard

Knowing your composure matters doesn’t make it easy to find mid-meltdown. Beyond the noise and flailing limbs, there is an emotional load. Watching someone you love in pain activates some of the same brain regions, including the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex, as feeling pain yourself. Without awareness of this response, or skills to manage it, a caregiver can get swept up in the very storm they are trying to weather.

Parents also often bring their own childhoods into the moment. Many of today’s parents were raised when compliance was prized over emotional literacy. A parent may be trying to respond with patience while a voice in their head insists, “I never would have gotten away with this.” That tension can fuel frustration, resentment, or self-doubt, making calm even harder to reach.

And plenty are running on low reserves. Across 11 Western countries, mothers and fathers spent more time directly caring for their children in 2012 than parents did in 1965. Child-centered, time-intensive parenting is now the ideal across social classes, whether or not families have the time and money to live up to it. Meanwhile, in a 2023 American Psychological Association survey, 48% of U.S. parents said their stress is completely overwhelming on most days, compared with 26% of other adults.

More time with our children has not translated into more well-being for parents. If staying grounded feels out of reach, that is not a personal failing. It is a widely shared strain.

The bigger picture: a generation still catching up

If self-regulation feels like a common topic among teachers and parents of young kids, you are not imagining it. In an October 2025 survey of more than 200 U.S. kindergarten teachers who use an early-literacy program from the education company Lexia, 82% said incoming students were less socially and emotionally ready than past classes, especially with sharing, collaboration, and emotion regulation. It was an opt-in survey, not a representative sample, but its findings line up with the pandemic-era research below.

Researchers are still sorting out the causes. One open question is whether earlier and heavier screen use displaces the face-to-face, back-and-forth interactions in which regulation is practiced. The COVID-19 pandemic is another likely contributor: several longitudinal studies have found that executive function growth slowed during school closures and lockdowns and has been sluggish to recover, with the clearest effects among children who were in or starting school at the time.

The message from this research is hopeful, though: with support, predictable routines, and opportunities to practice, children can still acquire these skills.

When is it time to get more help?

Toddlers show a wide range of behaviors—some have dramatic or exuberant tantrums, while others rarely do. When a parent is concerned that emotional or physical outbursts exceed the typical expression for age and development, a check-in with the pediatrician is in order.

Your pediatrician can look for physical contributors that lower a child's threshold for distress, including pain, poor or disrupted sleep, sensory sensitivity, hearing problems, constipation, or other concerns.

The pediatrician and caregiver can decide whether further assessment for conditions such as anxiety, ADHD, or autism would be useful. Several of these have been associated with atypical tantrum patterns in preschoolers. Executive function challenges and impulsivity, for example, are common in children with ADHD, and a diagnosis may provide validation and relief for some families. For children with autism, meltdowns may reflect heightened reactivity to sensory input and difficulty with change or unexpected demands. Understanding this can help parents frame a meltdown as overwhelm from a stressor rather than willful behavior. Some families, however, are reluctant to label young children or they find neurodevelopmental evaluation fraught; the right path depends on each family’s needs and preferences and is best worked out with the medical or developmental team.

The bottom line

Parents cannot make tantrums stop on command, but they can help build the brain that eventually learns to regulate them. Every time a caregiver lends their calm, the child practices the regulation skills they will one day use on their own. That means caring for your own reserves is an essential part of the work. If tantrums or meltdowns are frequent, prolonged, or unsafe, reaching out to explore medical and behavioral evaluation shows attunement and advocacy, not parental failure.

item.title: "Sources of Power": How the Book Came Into Being
item.description:
Decision-Making

"Sources of Power": How the Book Came Into Being

How a broken ankle led to a book.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • The book never would have gotten written if I had not broken my ankle — truly a lucky break.
  • Our data collection method revolved around stories of tough cases — these rich stories have their own power.
  • The book concept expanded from decision-making to cover macrocognition.
  • Publishing the book was insufficient for getting the word out — it required additional showcasing.

I published my book Sources of Power in 1998, and as of June 2026, it had sold over 72,000 copies, making it fairly successful as far as academic books go.

But why did I write it? And how did it get published? This is a good time to describe its origins.

In 1985, I began studying the way firefighters make tough decisions under time pressure and uncertainty. My colleagues Roberta Calderwood and Anne Clinton-Cirocco and I had gotten a small contract from the Army Research Institute to study firefighter decision-making, and we planned to observe firefighters in action. Unfortunately (or perhaps fortunately), that didn’t work out because building codes in the Dayton, Ohio area had been effective in preventing fires, so there was little to observe. Therefore, we changed our tactic and gathered data by asking highly experienced firefighters to tell us about their challenging cases. These stories generated the Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) model, which explained how firefighters could make decisions without spending time contrasting options. We presented our findings in a paper in 1986. We studied other types of decision makers and got confirming evidence, and I wrote these studies up (Klein, 1989a; Klein, 1989b).

And that was it. I had done the research, analyzed the data, and published the findings.

However, there was something missing. Our method yielded a set of compelling stories, and these stories hadn’t been told in the academic publications. The only way to do these stories justice was to write a book about them.

But I wasn’t a writer, and I didn’t have time to write a book, so it seemed unlikely that the book would ever happen.

Then I had a lucky break. Literally. My wife Helen had a sabbatical in Jerusalem in 1992-1993, and I tagged along. I didn’t have much to do, but I was happy to sightsee. Then one day I was jogging in a little valley behind our apartment building, thinking that it was only a matter of time before I injured myself because it wasn’t a proper path, just a rocky trail. Ten minutes later, I did come down wrong, twisted my ankle, and broke a bone in my ankle. I limped back to my apartment and realized my sightseeing days were over. I was immobilized.

Very depressing, except that to salvage my sanity, I decided that perhaps this was the opportunity to write that book about the stories.

I was due to return to the U.S. in a month. I calculated that if I could write 8 pages a day (single-spaced), I could finish a first draft of the book. Time to get working.

I spent a day or two just imagining the book, not writing at all. I made an outline of each chapter, including the stories I wanted to include (so that I wouldn’t tell the same story twice, or leave out any of the good ones). Next, I prepared a more detailed version of the outline. I was going to prepare an even more detailed version, but that was getting tedious. It was easier to turn to the writing.

I established a regimen. Before I went to sleep, I would review the material I wanted to cover the next day. I hoped that would give my subconscious mind something to chew on while I slept. When I got up, I was eager to get to my laptop. I kept to my schedule pretty well. And I finished the draft in the month I had allocated.

In the process of writing the book, the concept expanded because of the richness of the stories. Instead of just writing about decision-making, I also covered related topics such as problem solving, metaphors, and expertise. Other chapters explored how we read minds, the concept of a team mind, and hyper-rationality as the excesses of the Judgment and Decision Making perspective and of the Heuristics and Biases movement.

It turned into a book about naturalistic decision-making, although that wasn’t my original intent. It is a book about macrocognition, although we hadn’t conceptualized that yet. The stories just had more meaning than I had expected. Only seven out of the 17 chapters are about decision-making.

The book also described how to study cognition outside of a laboratory. And it highlighted the strengths of our decision-making, thus serving as a counter to the heuristics and biases movement that concentrated on flaws and failures.

I hope that people who are familiar with the judgment and decision-making approach will see the world differently after reading Sources of Power.

So that’s how the book got written. How did it get published? I didn’t have an agent, and I submitted the manuscript to an academic press, but they wanted more modifications than I wanted to make. Then my friend Robert Hoffman connected me with an editor at MIT Press, and that has worked out very well. They recently published the 20th anniversary edition of Sources of Power.

So that should be the end of the story. However, my colleague Mike McCloskey decided that the book deserved a wider readership. He contacted Tom Petzinger, a columnist at the Wall Street Journal. Petzinger was taken with the radical message of the RPD model and wrote two separate columns about Sources of Power, and these showcased the book to a side audience. Later, Malcolm Gladwell gave it some prominence in his book Blink.

So that’s the story of Sources of Power, a book motivated by the stories of the firefighters and military officers and others who make tough decisions under time pressure and uncertainty — and a broken ankle gave me the time to tell those stories.

item.title: Can We Protect Children Before Family Care Breaks Down?
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Can We Protect Children Before Family Care Breaks Down?

Research suggests child protection should begin before a family reaches crisis.

Posted October 16, 2026

Key points
  • Care deprivation is a process rather than a sudden event.
  • Legal thresholds for intervention can miss years of weakening care and support networks.
  • Opportunities exist to strengthen families before crisis.

This is Part I of a three-part series based on recent research by sociologist Tatevik Karapetyan, which focuses on reframing the idea of care deprivation within a family setting. Based on cases from the FAR Child Protection Center in Armenia, it identifies and names specific challenges that often go unseen and advocates for the identification of a variety of specific challenges and for earlier intervention.

“Could we have helped this child earlier?”

When you work with children and families in crisis, this painful question can linger even after successful interventions. Child protection systems are designed to respond when problems arise, such as neglect, inadequate parental care, or family crisis. At that point, social workers, courts, schools, or other institutions intervene.

However, in many cases we see at the FAR Child Protection Center in Armenia, the difficulties that brought the children to our door may have been developing for years. New research tries to reframe care deprivation in families as a process that develops over time. This may sound obvious to many onlookers, but there is a difference between that school of thought and the current definition of care deprivation, which is seen in the eyes of child protection systems as a status that is triggered by a specific event that requires our intervention. You are either care deprived and in need of intervention, or you are not. This binary choice often leaves children in precarious positions that may have been prevented. Measuring and defining elements such as the child’s extended care and support network and their legal status earlier may lead to better outcomes.

Stable families rarely slide into crisis overnight

Reliable relationships may weaken over time, or a parent may be physically present but less emotionally or practically available. Likewise, extended family connections and people who once helped fill the void may no longer be available. Financial pressure, illness, migration, violence, and unemployment are just a few of the many challenges that can pile up and eventually isolate a family that once had support.

The child may still be living in what appears to be a stable and reliable caregiving environment. No tangible event has drawn the attention of child protection services, nor have they crossed the threshold of any legal classification that requires intervention. But internally, the fabric of their social capital and those people they can depend on may be stretching thin and on the verge of tearing apart.

Recent research in Armenia by sociologist Tatevik Karapetyan highlights the need to focus on this period. Instead of viewing the loss of family care as a single event or legal status, her work frames it as a process that can begin well before a child enters the child protection system.

Karapetyan currently serves as a researcher and lecturer at Yerevan State University’s Chair of Social Work and Social Technologies and as Senior Programs Officer at the Armenian Association of Social Workers. Previously, she served as a quality assurance officer at the Fund for Armenian Relief's Mardigian Child Protection Center (CPC).

Karapetyan’s work focused on children deprived of family care using case records from CPC interviews with child protection professionals, and interviews with children themselves. Her study examined 239 family case histories from the CPC involving 321 children, alongside interviews with 10 key informants and 30 children. A quantitative analysis drew on a subset of 153 family cases involving 246 children. (Full disclosure: I was fortunate to serve as the scientific advisor on this project.)

Karapetyan’s perspective has significant implications for prevention and may help build systems and implement policies and procedures to identify issues earlier, leading to better outcomes for the child and their family.

Care deprivation is a process

The study distinguishes the social process of care deprivation from the outcome of family care deprivation. It's the difference between a dynamic, ongoing process and a static condition. In Karapetyan's model, key relationships may weaken, become distorted, disintegrate, and eventually rupture well before they gain the attention of child-protection services.

That distinction matters because child-protection systems function on specific categories and the criteria that define them. Formal decisions often depend on defined categories and thresholds, which may not fully capture the gradual changes in a child’s everyday care. A child either meets a threshold for intervention or does not; a child remains with a family or enters an alternative form of care.

While these categories are operationally and functionally necessary, they can downplay what occurred before a family crosses these thresholds. When we focus only on outcomes, it is easy to overlook the deterioration that led to them.

This raises a new question for social workers everywhere and others involved in child protection. What if the best opportunity to protect some children occurs before they officially need protection?

Moving child protection upstream

By viewing care deprivation as a process rather than a sudden event, there may be opportunities to strengthen families, repair relationships, restore resources, and prevent separation. We need to shift our objective from identifying more children as "at risk" to recognizing emerging vulnerabilities around a child and strengthening the relationships and resources that support their care.

Source: Fund for Armenian Relief

Sometimes the most successful child-protection intervention is the one that prevents a child from ever entering the child protection system.
